claim: Ebola virus disease (EVD) is a complex zoonosis that is highly virulent in humans.
source: Ebola virus disease (EVD) is a complex zoonosis that is highly virulent in humans.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about EVD that draws from established scientific understanding of the disease.

claim: The largest recorded outbreak of EVD is ongoing in West Africa, outside of its previously reported and predicted niche.
source: The largest recorded outbreak of EVD is ongoing in West Africa, outside of its previously reported and predicted niche.
evidence: This statement is supported by the context of the manuscript being written during the 2014 outbreak and references to previous predictions.

claim: The predicted zoonotic transmission niche covers 22 countries across Central and West Africa.
source: Using species distribution models, these occurrence data were paired with environmental covariates to predict a zoonotic transmission niche covering 22 countries across Central and West Africa.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vegetation, elevation, temperature, evapotranspiration, and suspected reservoir bat distributions define the relationship for zoonotic transmission.
source: Vegetation, elevation, temperature, evapotranspiration, and suspected reservoir bat distributions define this relationship.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the modeling analysis showing these covariates' contributions.

claim: At-risk areas are inhabited by 22 million people.
source: At-risk areas are inhabited by 22 million people
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and calculated from population data in the results.

claim: The rarity of human outbreaks emphasises the very low probability of transmission to humans.
source: however, the rarity of human outbreaks emphasises the very low probability of transmission to humans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that despite large at-risk populations, outbreaks are rare.

claim: Increasing population sizes and international connectivity by air since 1976 suggest that the dynamics of human-to-human secondary transmission in contemporary outbreaks will be very different to those of the past.
source: Increasing population sizes and international connectivity by air since the first detection of EVD in 1976 suggest that the dynamics of human-to-human secondary transmission in contemporary outbreaks will be very different to those of the past.
evidence: This is supported by data on population growth and airline connectivity presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ebola viruses have been responsible for outbreaks of EVD in humans for the last forty years.
source: Ebola viruses have for the last forty years been responsible for a number of outbreaks of Ebola virus disease (EVD) in humans (Pattyn et al., 1977)
evidence: This is supported by citation to historical literature and the temporal scope of the study.

claim: EVD has high case fatality rates typically around 60–70%, but potentially reaching as high as 90%.
source: with high case fatality rates typically around 60–70%, but potentially reaching as high as 90% (Feldmann and Geisbert, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature on EVD case fatality rates.

claim: The most recent outbreak began in Guinea in December 2013.
source: The most recent outbreak began in Guinea in December 2013 (Baize et al., 2014; Bausch and Schwarz, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published reports on the outbreak.

claim: The outbreak has subsequently spread to Liberia, Sierra Leone and Nigeria.
source: and has subsequently spread to Liberia, Sierra Leone and Nigeria (ECDC, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to ECDC reporting.

claim: The current outbreak was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 8 August 2014.
source: This has led to the current outbreak being declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on the 8 August 2014 (Briand et al., 2014; Gostin et al., 2014; WHO, 2014d).
evidence: This is supported by citations to WHO and other official declarations.

claim: Ebolavirus is a constituent genus of the Filoviridae family.
source: The Filoviridae, of which Ebolavirus is a constituent genus, belong to the order Mononegavirales.
evidence: This is a taxonomic classification statement based on established virology knowledge.

claim: Marburgvirus is responsible for a number of outbreaks of haemorrhagic fever across Africa.
source: Marburgvirus, itself responsible for a number of outbreaks of haemorrhagic fever across Africa (Gear et al., 1975; Conrad et al., 1978; Smith et al., 1982; Towner et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published outbreak reports.

claim: Cuevavirus was recently isolated from bats in northern Spain.
source: and Cuevavirus, recently isolated from bats in northern Spain (Negredo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the isolation report.

claim: Five species of Ebolavirus have been isolated to date.
source: Five species of Ebolavirus have been isolated to date (Kuhn et al., 2010; King et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to taxonomic references.

claim: The earliest recognised outbreaks of EVD were reported in Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo [DRC]) and Sudan in 1976.
source: the earliest recognised outbreaks of EVD were reported in Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo [DRC]) and Sudan in 1976 (International Commission, 1978; WHO International Study Team, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original outbreak investigation reports.

claim: The causative viruses from the 1976 outbreaks were isolated and later identified to be distinct species, Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV) and Sudan ebolavirus (SUDV).
source: The causative viruses were isolated (Pattyn et al., 1977) and later identified to be distinct species, Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV) and Sudan ebolavirus (SUDV).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the virus isolation and characterization work.

claim: Reston ebolavirus was isolated from Cynomologus monkeys imported from the Philippines to a facility in the United States, where they experienced severe haemorrhaging.
source: A third species of Ebolavirus, Reston ebolavirus, was isolated from Cynomologus monkeys imported from the Philippines to a facility in the United States, where they experienced severe haemorrhaging (Jahrling et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the isolation report.

claim: Serological evidence of infection with Reston ebolavirus has been reported in individuals in the Philippines.
source: Whilst serological evidence of infection with this species has been reported in individuals in the Philippines (Miranda et al., 1991)
evidence: This is supported by citation to serological survey data.

claim: No pathogenicity of Reston ebolavirus has been reported beyond primates and porcids.
source: no pathogenicity has been reported beyond primates and porcids (Barrette et al., 2009; Feldmann and Geisbert, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Reston ebolavirus pathogenicity.

claim: Tai Forest ebolavirus was isolated from a veterinarian who had autopsied a chimpanzee in Côte d'Ivoire in 1994.
source: In 1994 a fourth species, Tai Forest ebolavirus was isolated from a veterinarian who had autopsied a chimpanzee in Côte d'Ivoire (Le Guenno et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citation to the case report.

claim: Tai Forest ebolavirus has not been detected subsequently after 1994.
source: though the virus has not been detected subsequently.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of reported detections in the literature.

claim: Bundibugyo ebolavirus was responsible for an outbreak of EVD in Uganda in 2007.
source: The final species, Bundibugyo ebolavirus, was responsible for an outbreak of EVD in Uganda in 2007 (Towner et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to the outbreak investigation report.

claim: Bundibugyo ebolavirus was responsible for a more recent outbreak in the DRC.
source: as well as a more recent outbreak in the DRC (WHO, 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO outbreak reporting.

claim: Initial analysis suggested that the viruses isolated from the current outbreak, originating in Guinea, formed a separate clade within the five Ebolavirus species.
source: Initial analysis suggested that the viruses isolated from the current outbreak, originating in Guinea, formed a separate clade within the five Ebolavirus species (Baize et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the initial phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Subsequent re-analysis indicated that Guinea isolates nest within the Zaire ebolavirus lineage.
source: Subsequent re-analysis of the same sequences however, indicated that these isolates instead nest within the Zaire ebolavirus lineage (Dudas and Rambaut, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to the re-analysis.

claim: Guinea isolates diverged from Central Africa strains approximately ten years ago.
source: and diverged from Central Africa strains approximately ten years ago (Gire et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to phylogenetic dating analysis.

claim: Which reservoir species are responsible for maintaining Ebola transmission between outbreaks is not well understood.
source: Which reservoir species are responsible for maintaining Ebola transmission between outbreaks is not well understood (Peterson et al., 2004b)
evidence: This is supported by citation and reflects the state of knowledge at the time.

claim: Significant progress has been made in narrowing down the list of likely reservoir hosts over the last decade.
source: but over the last decade significant progress has been made in narrowing down the list of likely hosts (Peterson et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to review of reservoir research.

claim: Primates have long been known to harbour filoviral infections.
source: Primates have long been known to harbour filoviral infections, with the first Marburg strains identified in African green monkeys in 1967 (Siegert et al., 1967; Beer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical isolation reports.

claim: Significant mortality has been reported in wild primate populations across Africa, most notably in gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) and chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) populations.
source: Significant mortality has also been reported in wild primate populations across Africa, most notably in gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) and chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) populations (Formenty et al., 1999; Rouquet et al., 2005; Bermejo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to field studies documenting primate mortality.

claim: The high case fatality rates recorded in the great apes combined with their declining populations and limited geographical range indicate they are likely dead-end hosts for the virus and not reservoir species.
source: The high case fatality rates recorded in the great apes combined with their declining populations and limited geographical range, indicate they are likely dead-end hosts for the virus and not reservoir species (Groseth et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to analysis of great ape epidemiology.

claim: A large survey of small mammals in and around Gabon identified three species of bats which were infected with Ebola viruses—Hypsignathus monstrosus, Epomops franqueti and Myonycetris torquata.
source: A large survey of small mammals in and around Gabon identified three species of bats which were infected with Ebola viruses—Hypsignathus monstrosus, Epomops franqueti and Myonycetris torquata (Leroy et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the survey study.

claim: Subsequent serological surveys lend support to the hypothesis of a bat reservoir.
source: Subsequent serological surveys (Pourrut et al., 2009; Hayman et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to serological studies.

claim: Evidence linking the potential source of human outbreaks to bats lends support to the hypothesis of a bat reservoir.
source: and evidence linking the potential source of human outbreaks to bats (Leroy et al., 2009) lend support to the hypothesis of a bat reservoir.
evidence: This is supported by citation to epidemiological investigation.

claim: Marburgvirus has been repeatedly detected in the fruit bat Rousettus aegypticus.
source: This, coupled with repeated detection of Marburgvirus in the fruit bat Rousettus aegypticus (Towner et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to detection studies.

claim: The only isolations of Cuevavirus have been from bats (specifically Llovia virus).
source: and the only isolations of Cuevavirus also from bats (specifically Llovia virus [Negredo et al., 2011])
evidence: This is supported by citation to the isolation report.

claim: All evidence supports the suspicion that Chiroptera play an important role in the natural life-cycle of the filoviruses.
source: all support the suspicion that Chiroptera play an important role in the natural life-cycle of the filoviruses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple lines of evidence cited in the text.

claim: Humans represent a dead-end host for the virus.
source: Humans represent a dead-end host for the virus, with only stuttering chains of transmission reported between humans in the majority of previous outbreaks (Chowell et al., 2004; Legrand et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to transmission dynamics studies.

claim: There is no indication that humans can reintroduce the virus back into reservoir species.
source: and no indication that humans can reintroduce the virus back into reservoir species (Karesh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to ecological analysis.

claim: The incubation period in humans ranges from two days to three weeks.
source: The incubation period in humans ranges from two days to three weeks
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about EVD.

claim: At the peak of illness, haemorrhaging shock and widespread tissue damage can occur and can eventually lead to death within 6–16 days.
source: At the peak of illness, haemorrhaging shock and widespread tissue damage can occur and can eventually lead to death within 6–16 days (Feldmann and Geisbert, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical review.

claim: Human-to-human transmission is mainly through direct unprotected contact with infected individuals and cadavers.
source: Human-to-human transmission is mainly through direct unprotected contact with infected individuals and cadavers, with infectious particles detected in a number of different body fluids (Feldmann and Geisbert, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to transmission studies.

claim: The typical outbreak profile is defined by an index individual that has recently come into contact with the blood of another mammal through either hunting or the butchering of animal carcasses.
source: The typical outbreak profile is defined by an index individual that has recently come into contact with the blood of another mammal through either hunting or the butchering of animal carcasses (Pourrut et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to epidemiological analysis.

claim: A recurring theme of hunting and handling bushmeat is suspected as the source for index cases.
source: Whilst it has been difficult to identify the zoonotic source for the index cases of some outbreaks, a recurring theme of hunting and handling bushmeat is suspected (Table 1; Boumandouki et al., 2005; Nkoghe et al., 2005, 2011; Leroy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to outbreak investigations and reference to Table 1.

claim: The highest risk activities for human-to-human transmission are those that bring humans into close contact with infected individuals.
source: In subsequent human-to-human transmission, the highest risk activities are those that bring humans into close contact with infected individuals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EVD transmission dynamics.

claim: High risk activities include medical settings where insufficient infection control precautions have been taken, as well as home care and funeral preparations carried out by families or close friends.
source: These include medical settings where insufficient infection control precautions have been taken, as well as home care and funeral preparations carried out by families or close friends (Baron et al., 1983; Georges et al., 1999; Boumandouki et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to outbreak investigations documenting transmission routes.

claim: Chains of infection typically do not exceed three or four sequential transmission events.
source: Typically, chains of infection do not exceed three or four sequential transmission events
evidence: This is an inference from historical outbreak data.

claim: In the outbreak in Gabon in 1996, a single person was responsible for infecting ten other individuals.
source: In the outbreak in Gabon in 1996, a single person was responsible for infecting ten other individuals (Milleliri et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to outbreak investigation.

claim: In the 1995 outbreak in the DRC, thirty five cases resulted from one individual.
source: whilst in the 1995 outbreak in the DRC, thirty five cases resulted from one individual (Khan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to outbreak investigation.

claim: Secondary transmission can be restricted by effective case detection and isolation measures.
source: Secondary transmission can be restricted by effective case detection and isolation measures (Shoemaker et al., 2012; WHO, 2014c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to outbreak control studies.

claim: Where effective case detection and isolation cannot be achieved, secondary cases can continue to occur.
source: Where this cannot be achieved, either due to a lack of infrastructure, poor understanding of the disease, or distrust of medical practices, secondary cases can continue to occur (Khan et al., 1999; Larkin, 2003; Hewlett et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to outbreak investigations.

claim: 23 outbreaks of Ebola virus were identified in humans across Africa.
source: In total, 23 outbreaks of Ebola virus were identified in humans across Africa, consisting of a hypothesised 30 independent primary infection events (Table 1; Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: The 23 outbreaks consist of a hypothesised 30 independent primary infection events.
source: In total, 23 outbreaks of Ebola virus were identified in humans across Africa, consisting of a hypothesised 30 independent primary infection events (Table 1; Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: The outbreaks span the last 40 years from the first outbreaks in 1976 to the five outbreaks that have occurred since 2010.
source: These outbreaks span the last 40 years from the first outbreaks in 1976 to the five outbreaks that have occurred since 2010 (Table 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by Table 1.

claim: Before December 2013, a total of 2322 cases had occurred from Ebolavirus infections.
source: Before December 2013, a total of 2322 cases had occurred from Ebolavirus infections, a number already overtaken by the likely underreported current case count of the ongoing outbreak >2250 (WHO, 2014a) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by Figure 2A and WHO citation.

claim: The current outbreak case count is >2250 and is likely underreported.
source: a number already overtaken by the likely underreported current case count of the ongoing outbreak >2250 (WHO, 2014a)
evidence: This is supported by WHO citation and inference about underreporting.

claim: Zaire ebolavirus has been responsible for the most outbreaks (13).
source: Of the four viruses circulating in Africa, Zaire ebolavirus has been responsible for the most outbreaks (13)
evidence: This is derived from counting outbreaks in the compiled dataset.

claim: Sudan ebolavirus has been responsible for 7 outbreaks.
source: followed by Sudan ebolavirus (7)
evidence: This is derived from counting outbreaks in the compiled dataset.

claim: Bundibugyo ebolavirus has caused two outbreaks in 2007/8 and 2012.
source: and Bundigbuyo ebolavirus with just two outbreaks in 2007/8 and 2012.
evidence: This is derived from counting outbreaks in the compiled dataset.

claim: Tai Forest has caused one confirmed infection in humans, from which the patient recovered.
source: Tai Forest has caused one confirmed infection in humans, from which the patient recovered (Le Guenno et al., 1995; Formenty et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the case report.

claim: There was an absence of reported outbreaks in humans for 15 years between 1979 and 1994.
source: Although outbreaks have been reported since 1976, there was an absence of reported outbreaks in humans for 15 years between 1979 and 1994 (although antibodies in humans were identified over the period [Kuhn, 2008])
evidence: This is derived from the outbreak timeline and supported by citation.

claim: The frequency of outbreaks has increased substantially post 2000.
source: and the frequency of outbreaks has increased substantially post 2000 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and stated in the text.

claim: A total of 51 surveyed locations reporting infections in animals were identified in the literature since the discovery of the disease.
source: A total of 51 surveyed locations reporting infections in animals were identified in the literature since the discovery of the disease (Table 2; Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: The 51 animal infection locations comprised 17 infections in gorillas (Gorilla gorilla), nine infections in chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), 18 in OWFB and 2 in duikers (Cephalophus spp.).
source: These comprised 17 infections in gorillas (Gorilla gorilla), nine infections in chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), 18 in OWFB and 2 in duikers (Cephalophus spp.).
evidence: This is derived from the compiled animal infection dataset.

claim: A large proportion of the great ape cases originated from the ROC/Gabon border.
source: A large proportion of the great ape cases originated from the ROC/Gabon border, coinciding with the main known distributions of both chimpanzees and gorillas (Petter and Desbordes, 2013)
evidence: This is derived from the geographic distribution of cases and supported by citation to species distribution reference.

claim: The great ape cases represent a period of well-documented great ape Ebola outbreaks in and around the Lossi Animal Sanctuary.
source: and representing a period of well-documented great ape Ebola outbreaks in and around the Lossi Animal Sanctuary (Rouquet et al., 2005; Bermejo et al., 2006; Walsh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to field studies.

claim: All animal isolations of Ebola viruses have come from countries that have also reported index cases of human outbreaks, with the exception of several seropositive bats from a survey in southern Ghana.
source: All animal isolations of Ebola viruses have come from countries that have also reported index cases of human outbreaks, with the exception of several seropositive bats from a survey in southern Ghana.
evidence: This is derived from comparing the geographic distributions of animal and human cases.

claim: Distribution models for H. monstrosus demonstrated predictive skill with AUC 0.63 ± 0.04.
source: Distribution models for all three species demonstrated predictive skill (indicated by an area under the curve (AUC) greater than 0.5) as follows: H. monstrosus AUC 0.63 ± 0.04
evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claim: Distribution models for M. torquata demonstrated predictive skill with AUC = 0.59 ± 0.04.
source: M. torquata AUC = 0.59 ± 0.04
evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claim: Distribution models for E. franqueti demonstrated predictive skill with AUC = 0.58 ± 0.03.
source: E. franqueti AUC = 0.58 ± 0.03, n = 50 submodels for all three species.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claim: Each bat species was broadly predicted within its considered expert opinion range.
source: In addition, each species was broadly predicted within its considered expert opinion range (Figure 4A–C) (Schipper et al., 2008).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and supported by citation to expert range maps.

claim: The marginal effect plots for bat distributions were strongly influenced by land surface temperature (LST) and vegetation (as measured by the enhanced vegetation index [EVI]).
source: The marginal effect plots (not shown) were strongly influenced by land surface temperature (LST) and vegetation (as measured by the enhanced vegetation index [EVI]).
evidence: This is derived from the modeling analysis.

claim: The predicted combined distribution of the three bat species covers West and Central Africa, specifically the moist forests of the northeastern, western and central Congo basin, and Guinea, as well as the Congolian coastal forest ecoregions.
source: The predicted combined distribution of these species (Figure 4D), covers West and Central Africa, specifically the moist forests of the northeastern, western and central Congo basin, and Guinea, as well as the Congolian coastal forest ecoregions (WWF, 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and described in the text with reference to ecoregion classification.

claim: All countries with observed index cases of EVD (n = 7, Set 1) have areas of the highest environmental suitability.
source: All countries with observed index cases of EVD (n = 7, hereafter Set 1) have areas of the highest environmental suitability (see list in Table 1).
evidence: This is derived from the modeling results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Areas of high environmental suitability for zoonotic transmission are predicted in a further 15 countries where index cases of the four African species of Ebolavirus have not been recorded.
source: In addition, areas of high environmental suitability for zoonotic transmission are predicted in a further 15 countries where, to date, index cases of the four African species of Ebolavirus have not been recorded.
evidence: This is derived from the modeling results.

claim: The 15 countries without recorded index cases but with predicted high suitability (Set 2) are Nigeria, Cameroon, Central African Republic (CAR), Ghana, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Angola, Tanzania, Togo, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Burundi, Equatorial Guinea, Madagascar and Malawi.
source: These are Nigeria, Cameroon, Central African Republic (CAR), Ghana, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Angola, Tanzania, Togo, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Burundi, Equatorial Guinea, Madagascar and Malawi (hereafter Set 2).
evidence: This is directly stated as the list of Set 2 countries.

claim: The AUC for the Ebola model was 0.85 ± 0.04.
source: The AUC for the Ebola model was relatively high (AUC = 0.85 ± 0.04, n = 500 submodels)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claim: The Ebola model could strongly distinguish regions of environmental suitability for EVD.
source: indicating that the model could strongly distinguish regions of environmental suitability for EVD.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the AUC statistic.

claim: Enhanced vegetation index had the greatest impact on the Ebola distribution with relative contribution of 65.3%.
source: Enhanced vegetation index had the greatest impact on the distribution (relative contribution [RC] of 65.3%)

claim: Elevation had a relative contribution of 11.7% to the Ebola distribution model.
source: followed by elevation (RC = 11.7%)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claim: Night-time land surface temperature (LST) had a relative contribution of 7.7% to the Ebola distribution model.
source: night-time land surface temperature (LST) (RC = 7.7%)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claim: Potential evapotranspiration (PET) had a relative contribution of 5.7% to the Ebola distribution model.
source: potential evapotranspiration (PET) (RC = 5.7%)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claim: Combined bat distribution had a relative contribution of 3.8% to the Ebola distribution model.
source: and combined bat distribution (RC = 3.8%).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claim: In total, 22.2 million people are predicted to live in areas suitable for zoonotic transmission of Ebola.
source: In total, 22.2 million people are predicted to live in areas suitable for zoonotic transmission of Ebola.
evidence: This is calculated from population data overlaid on the predicted distribution.

claim: The vast majority, 21.7 million (approximately 97%), live in rural areas, as opposed to urban or peri-urban areas.
source: The vast majority, 21.7 million (approximately 97%), live in rural areas, as opposed to urban or peri-urban areas (CIESIN/IFPRI/WB/CIAT, 2007; WorldPop, 2014).

claim: Of the 22.2 million people at risk, 15.2 million are in Set 1 and 7 million are in Set 2.
source: Of these, 15.2 million are in Set 1 and 7 million are in Set 2.

claim: In terms of ranked populations at risk, DRC, Guinea and Uganda are highest in Set 1.
source: In terms of ranked populations at risk, DRC, Guinea and Uganda are highest in Set 1

claim: Nigeria, Cameroon and CAR have the highest populations at risk in Set 2.
source: and Nigeria, Cameroon and CAR are top in Set 2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Over the 40 year period since discovery of EVD, the total population living in those countries predicted to be within the zoonotic niche has nearly tripled (from 230 million to 639 million).
source: Over the 40 year period since discovery of EVD, the total population living in those countries predicted to be within the zoonotic niche has nearly tripled (from 230 million to 639 million)
evidence: This is calculated from World Bank population data.

claim: The proportion of the population in at-risk countries living in an urban (rather than rural) setting has changed from 25.5% to 59.2% over 40 years.
source: and the proportion of the population in these countries living in an urban (rather than rural) setting has changed from 25.5% to 59.2% (Figure 6).
evidence: This is calculated from World Bank population data and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Rates of population movement within a country will scale directly in proportion to population growth.
source: We can infer however, intuitively, empirically and theoretically (Zipf, 1946; Simini et al., 2012) that rates of population movement within a country will scale directly in proportion to population growth.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to mobility theory.

claim: Passenger seat capacity in Set 1 countries increased from 2.96 to 4.77 million between 2000 and 2013, a fractional change of 1.61.
source: Records of passenger seat capacity are available since 2000 and show substantive increases over the period in Set 1 (from 2.96 to 4.77 million, a fractional change of 1.61)

source: The largest increases have occurred in WHO regions (WHO, 2014b) outside of the sub-Saharan African region (AFRO) (Figure 8A,B).

claim: In 2012, almost half of the final destinations of those travelling from at-risk countries were to other AFRO nations (47%).
source: In 2012, almost half of the final destinations of those travelling from these at-risk countries were to other AFRO nations (47%).

claim: The zoonotic niche map delineates areas in which populations are at-risk of zoonotic transmission of EVD.
source: It is important to appreciate that this zoonotic niche map delineates areas in which populations are at-risk of zoonotic transmission of EVD (Figure 5B).

evidence: This is a clarification of the limitations of the map.

claim: Increasing human encroachment and certain cultural practices sometimes linked with poverty, such as bushmeat hunting, result in increasing exposure of humans to animals which may harbour diseases including Ebola.
source: Increasing human encroachment and certain cultural practices sometimes linked with poverty, such as bushmeat hunting, result in increasing exposure of humans to animals which may harbour diseases including Ebola (Daszak, 2000; Wolfe et al., 2005, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on zoonotic disease emergence.

claim: The modeling process accommodates uncertainty in geopositioning of index cases by utilising both point and polygon data.
source: Furthermore, our modelling process accommodates uncertainty in geopositioning of these index cases by utilising both point and polygon data.
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the analysis.

claim: The dataset used in the model increased to 81 occurrences by including occurrence of infection in wildlife.
source: In addition, we include occurrence of infection in wildlife, important to the wider scale of zoonotic transmission (Figure 1), which in total has increased the dataset used in the model to 81 occurrences.
evidence: This describes the composition of the modeling dataset.

claim: The rareness of EVD outbreaks and the prevalence of detectable Ebola virus in reservoir species suggests that there will always be a limited set of observation data when compared to mapping of more prevalent zoonoses.
source: The rareness of EVD outbreaks and the prevalence of detectable Ebola virus in reservoir species suggests that there will always be a limited set of observation data when compared to mapping of more prevalent zoonoses (Pigott et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference about data limitations supported by citation.

claim: A broad zoonotic niche is predicted across 22 countries in Central and West Africa.
source: A broad zoonotic niche is predicted across 22 countries in Central and West Africa.
evidence: This summarizes the main modeling result.

claim: Serological evidence in some regions points to possible underreporting of small-scale outbreaks.
source: Whilst several of these countries have reported index cases of EVD, others have not, although serological evidence in some regions points to possible underreporting of small-scale outbreaks (Kuhn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to serological survey review.

claim: Despite a relatively large population living in areas of risk and the widespread practice of bushmeat hunting in these predicted areas, Ebolavirus is rare both in suspected animal reservoirs and in terms of human outbreaks.
source: Despite relatively a large population living in areas of risk and the widespread practice of bushmeat hunting in these predicted areas (Wolfe et al., 2005; Mfunda and Røskaft, 2010; Brashares et al., 2011; Kamins et al., 2011), Ebolavirus is rare both in suspected animal reservoirs (Leroy et al., 2005; Olival and Hayman, 2014) and in terms of human outbreaks (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to bushmeat hunting studies and reservoir surveys, and reference to Table 1.

claim: There is some indication that the frequency of Ebola outbreaks has increased since 2000.
source: There is some indication however, that the frequency of Ebola outbreaks has increased since 2000, as shown in Figure 2A.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The human population living within the zoonotic niche is larger, more mobile and better internationally connected than when the pathogen was first observed.
source: We have shown that the human population living within this niche is larger, more mobile and better internationally connected than when the pathogen was first observed.
evidence: This is supported by the demographic and mobility analyses presented.

claim: When spillover events occur, the likelihood of continued spread amongst the human population is greater, particularly in areas with poor healthcare infrastructure.
source: As a result, when spillover events do occur, the likelihood of continued spread amongst the human population is greater, particularly in areas with poor healthcare infrastructure (Briand et al., 2014; Fauci, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to outbreak analyses.

claim: Ebola outbreaks can have a considerable economic and political impact.
source: Whilst rare in comparison to other high burden diseases prevalent in this region, such as malaria (Gething et al., 2011; Murray et al., 2012), Ebola outbreaks can have a considerable economic and political impact
evidence: This is supported by citations to disease burden studies and general knowledge.

claim: The destabilisation of basic health care provisioning in affected regions increases the toll of unrecorded morbidity and mortality of more common infectious diseases throughout and after the epidemic period.
source: and the subsequent destabilisation of basic health care provisioning in affected regions increases the toll of unrecorded morbidity and mortality of more common infectious diseases (Murray et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014), throughout and after the epidemic period.
evidence: This is supported by citations to health systems impact studies.

claim: The number of concurrent infections during the present outbreak represents a significant strain on healthcare systems that are already poorly provisioned.
source: The number of concurrent infections during the present outbreak represents a significant strain on healthcare systems that are already poorly provisioned (Briand et al., 2014; Chan, 2014; Fauci, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to outbreak response analyses.

claim: Many Set 1 and Set 2 countries rank amongst the lowest per capita healthcare spenders.
source: and many other Set 1 and Set 2 countries rank amongst the lowest per capita healthcare spenders.
evidence: This is an inference from general knowledge about healthcare spending in these countries.

claim: The increasing connectedness of the Africa region means that EVD is now a problem of international concern.
source: The increasing connectedness of the Africa region means that EVD is now a problem of international concern.
evidence: This is an inference from the connectivity data presented.

claim: Most EVD secondary transmission occurs locally and is likely transported via ground transit.
source: While most EVD secondary transmission occurs locally and is likely transported via ground transit (Francesconi et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to transmission study.

claim: The potential for international spread of infection is possible, as demonstrated by the importation of the disease from Liberia to Nigeria, culminating in further secondary transmission in Lagos.
source: the potential for international spread of infection is possible, as demonstrated by the importation of the disease from Liberia to Nigeria, culminating in further secondary transmission in Lagos (WHO, 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO outbreak reporting.

claim: The aetiology of EVD infection and disease progression means that an international outbreak propagated by air travel remains unlikely, particularly in high-income countries better able to handle EVD cases.
source: The aetiology of EVD infection and disease progression means that an international outbreak propagated by air travel remains unlikely, particularly in high-income countries better able to handle EVD cases (Fauci, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to outbreak analysis.

claim: A non-negligible threat of international spread remains, particularly in the low and middle income destinations.
source: Nevertheless, a non-negligible threat remains, particularly in the low and middle income destinations
evidence: This is an inference from the connectivity and healthcare capacity data.

claim: The rapid increase in global connectivity of at-risk regions indicates that international airports could see more imported cases.
source: and the rapid increase in global connectivity of these at-risk regions indicates that international airports could see more imported cases (Chan, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation and connectivity data.

claim: Analysis excluding the Guinea outbreak from the training dataset still resulted in prediction of high suitability in the Guinea region, with the presumed index village located within 5 km of an at-risk pixel.
source: Further analysis, excluding the existing outbreak focussed in Guinea from the dataset used to train the model (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), still resulted in prediction of high suitability in this region, with the presumed index village located within 5 km of an at-risk pixel.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and described in the text.

claim: The eco-epidemiological situation in Guinea is very similar to that in past outbreaks, mirroring phylogenetic similarity in the causative viruses.
source: This implies that the eco-epidemiological situation in Guinea is very similar to that in past outbreaks, mirroring phylogenetic similarity in the causative viruses (Dudas and Rambaut, 2014; Gire et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The ecological similarity between the past and current outbreaks lends support to the notion that the scale of this outbreak is more heavily influenced by patterns of human-to-human transmission than any expansion of the zoonotic niche.
source: The ecological similarity between the past and current outbreaks also lends support to the notion that the scale of this outbreak is more heavily influenced by patterns of human-to-human transmission than any expansion of the zoonotic niche.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results and outbreak characteristics.

claim: A boosted regression tree (BRT) modelling framework was used to generate predictive risk maps of the zoonotic Ebola virus niche in Africa.
source: A boosted regression tree (BRT) modelling framework was used to generate predictive risk maps of the zoonotic Ebola virus niche in Africa.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach.

claim: This study was limited to the African continent since no natural outbreaks of EVD have occurred outside the continent.
source: This study was limited to the African continent since no natural outbreaks of EVD have occurred outside the continent (CDC, 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citation.

claim: Reston ebolavirus has a distribution reported outside of Africa, focussed in the Philippines, but has never been reported as pathogenic in humans.
source: Only Reston ebolavirus has a distribution reported outside of Africa, focussed in the Philippines, but has never been reported as pathogenic in humans; as a result this species was not included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on established knowledge.

claim: 239 locations were identified from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) for the three bat species: 67 for H. monstrosus, 52 for M. torquata and 120 for E. franqueti.
source: In total, 239 locations were identified from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) (GBIF, 2014): 67 for H. monstrosus (Figure 4A), 52 for M. torquata (Figure 4B) and 120 for E. franqueti (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes the bat occurrence dataset used in modeling.

claim: A pixel was assumed to be at risk if its predicted environmental suitability for zoonotic Ebola virus transmission was greater than 0.673, the lowest suitability value predicted at the locations of known transmission to humans.
source: A pixel was assumed to be at risk if its predicted environmental suitability for zoonotic Ebola virus transmission was greater than 0.673, the lowest suitability value predicted at the locations of known transmission to humans (point records of human index cases).
evidence: This describes the thresholding method used to define at-risk areas.
